q205: Sometimes your body rings a fire alarm when there is no fire. If you breathe slowly and stay, the alarm goes quiet, and God is with you the whole time.
q206: Mercy and the phone that never rang
q207: Mercy, 56, retired nurse in Kottayam, Kerala, with two sons working in the Gulf
q208: Mercy's two sons work in Dubai and Muscat, and her daughter is studying in Chennai. Every evening she waited for their calls. If one son did not reply to her WhatsApp message within an hour, her mind ran wild. Had there been an accident at the site? Was he ill and hiding it? She would call him again and again until he answered, sometimes annoyed. She checked the news from the Gulf several times a day. Her husband said she was making herself sick, and he was partly right. She had headaches, a sour stomach and woke at three in the morning to pray, but her prayers felt more like panic than trust. Her younger son finally told her gently that her calls made him feel like a child.
q209: Worry feels like love, and it often starts from love. But Mercy's brain had learned that worrying was a way of keeping her children safe, as if thinking about every danger could prevent it. Psychologists call this intolerance of uncertainty: the mind cannot rest until it knows for sure that everyone is fine. Each reassuring call gave short relief, but it also taught her brain that calling was the only way to calm down. Her years as a nurse had trained her to spot what could go wrong. Behind it all was an older story. Her own father had died suddenly when she was twelve, and nobody had told her until two days later.
q210: In a quiet talk with her pastor's wife, Mercy said aloud, I think if I stop worrying, something bad will happen. Hearing herself say it, she saw that she had made worry into a kind of guard. She realised she was trusting her worry more than she was trusting God.
q211: Set a daily worry time of fifteen minutes at five in the evening with a notebook
q212: Used the worry tree to sort worries into ones she could act on and ones she could only pray about
q213: Agreed with her sons on one fixed call each week plus a simple thumbs-up message each night
q214: Turned each leftover worry into a short breath prayer, such as Lord, You are with Joel
q215: Limited Gulf news to once a day
q216: Jesus asked a simple question: which of you by taking thought can add one cubit unto his stature (Matthew 6:27). Worry cannot protect our children. Only God can. Paul does not say we will have nothing to worry about. He says to bring everything to God in prayer with thanksgiving, and the peace of God will keep our hearts and minds (Philippians 4:6-7). The word keep is a military word, like a guard at a gate. Mercy had been standing guard herself. Now she could hand the watch back to God. Hannah gave Samuel to the Lord and left him at the temple (1 Samuel 1:27-28). Releasing children into God's hands is an ancient act of faith, not neglect.
q217: God designed the mind to plan and solve problems. Worry is that ability stuck in a loop, solving the same problem that has no answer today. Research suggests that setting aside a fixed time for worry can reduce how much it spills into the rest of the day, because the brain learns there is a place to put it. Writing worries down also seems to free up mental space. Slow breathing paired with a short prayer calms the stress response and gives the thinking brain a chance to come back online. We were made to carry today's load, not every possible tomorrow.
q218: Philippians 4:6|Be careful for nothing, but in every thing by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known unto God.
q222: Mercy still worries, especially during Gulf heatwaves or news of accidents. But the three in the morning wake-ups became rare, and her stomach settled. Her sons now call more freely because the calls are not tense. Twice she slipped back into repeated calling, and each time she noticed, smiled at herself and returned to her worry notebook.
q223: Worry is love trying to do God's job, and peace comes when we give the job back to Him.
q224: Worrying does not keep the people we love safe. Talking to God about them and trusting Him helps our hearts feel calm.
q226: Rajesh, 44, former production supervisor in Pune, married with two teenage children
q227: After nineteen years at the same auto parts factory, Rajesh was called into a room and told his post no longer existed. He came home with a cardboard box and could not look at his wife. For the first few weeks he applied for jobs every day. Then the replies stopped coming and so did his energy. He slept till ten, sat in front of the television and stopped going to church because people would ask what he was doing now. He snapped at his son over small things. Food lost its taste. One night his wife found him sitting on the terrace at two in the morning, and he told her quietly that the family would be better off without him.
q228: Job loss is one of the most painful life events, because for many men in India work is tied to identity, honour and being a good provider. When that is taken away, the brain can treat it like a deep loss. Depression is more than sadness. Research suggests that long stress and loss can change sleep, appetite and the reward system, so that things which once felt good feel flat. Withdrawal then removes the very things that might lift mood, such as friends, sunlight and movement, and the low mood deepens. Rajesh's belief was that a man who cannot provide has no worth. His thoughts of not wanting to live were a sign of serious depression that needed medical care, not a sign of weak faith.
q229: His wife did not argue or preach. She held his hand, called their pastor and the next morning took him to a psychiatrist. Rajesh was afraid of being called mad, but the doctor said, You are not weak, you are unwell, and this is treatable. That sentence felt like a door opening.
q230: Saw a psychiatrist, started prescribed medicine and agreed a safety plan with his wife
q231: Began weekly sessions with a Christian counsellor
q232: Planned one small activity each morning, such as a walk to buy milk, even without feeling like it
q233: Walked twenty minutes daily with a friend from church
q234: Wrote his own lament psalm telling God honestly how he felt
q235: Called two old colleagues using a simple reach-out script
q236: Elijah, after a great victory, ran into the desert and asked God to take his life (1 Kings 19:4). God did not scold him. He sent an angel who gave him food, water and sleep, and later spoke to him in a still small voice. God cared for Elijah's body first, then his heart, then gave him a new task. Rajesh's worth was never in his job title. He is a son of God, bought with a price (1 Corinthians 6:20). The psalmists cried out from the pit (Psalm 88), and God kept their honest prayers in the Bible for people like Rajesh. Getting medical help was not a lack of faith. It was receiving God's care through the hands of others.
q237: God designed our brains to respond to action, not only to feelings. In depression we wait to feel motivated before we act, but research suggests it often works the other way: small actions come first and mood slowly follows. This is called behavioural activation, and in studies it helps many people with depression. Walking and sunlight support the body's mood chemistry and sleep rhythm. Medicine, when a doctor prescribes it, can help a brain stuck in a deep low to function again. And we were made for connection. Being with people who care calms the stress system and reminds us we belong.
q238: Psalm 34:18|The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart, and saveth such as be of a contrite spirit.
q242: Recovery was slow. After two months Rajesh was sleeping better and the dark thoughts had faded, though some weeks were heavy again. After seven months he took a lower-paid job training apprentices, and found he loved teaching. He still sees his counsellor monthly and tells other men at church that seeing a doctor was the bravest thing he did.
q243: When life takes away our role, God reminds us of our identity, and getting help is part of how He carries us.
q244: Losing a job can make a heart very sad and tired. Doctors, friends and God can all help it slowly feel better again.
q245: Sunil and the shouting at homework time
q246: Sunil, 38, sales manager in Hyderabad, father of a son aged 9 and a daughter aged 6
q247: Every evening around eight, homework time turned into a war. Sunil came home tired from targets and traffic, and when his son dawdled over maths or his daughter spilled milk, he exploded. He shouted, slammed the table and once threw a school bag across the room. The children went silent and his wife took them into the bedroom. Afterwards Sunil felt sick with guilt and lay awake promising himself it would not happen again. Then the next evening it did. His daughter began flinching when he raised his voice even slightly. One Sunday at church, during a sermon on fathers, he had to step outside because he could not stop his tears. He had grown up with a father who beat him, and he had sworn never to be like him.
q248: Anger is often a secondary emotion sitting on top of others, like tiredness, fear, shame or feeling disrespected. By eight in the evening Sunil's stress bucket was full. A stressed brain can lose access to the prefrontal cortex, the calm thinking part, and the alarm system takes over in seconds. Some people call this flipping your lid. His children's normal childish behaviour triggered old memories stored in his body from his own childhood, when mistakes meant danger. Underneath his shouting was a belief that if his children did not perform, he was failing as a father, just as his own father had seen him as a failure.
q249: After one bad evening his son wrote on a paper, Papa, I am scared of you. Sunil sat on the floor with that paper for a long time. He did not want to excuse himself or crush himself. He wanted to change. He asked his wife to help him find a counsellor.
q250: Used the STOP skill when he felt heat in his chest, stepping out of the room for two minutes
q251: Took ten quiet minutes in the car before entering the house
q252: Wrote down what was under his anger each night, such as tired, afraid or ashamed
q253: Repaired with the children after every outburst, saying sorry without blaming them
q254: Moved from correcting first to connecting first at homework time
q255: Saw a counsellor to work on memories of his own father
q256: The Bible does not say anger itself is sin. It says be angry and sin not (Ephesians 4:26). But it warns fathers, provoke not your children to wrath, but bring them up in the nurture of the Lord (Ephesians 6:4). James tells us to be slow to speak, slow to wrath, for the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God (James 1:19-20). Sunil found hope in God the Father, who is slow to anger and plenteous in mercy (Psalm 103:8-13). As he received that patient love himself, he had more patience to give. Saying sorry to his children did not lower him as a father. It showed them what a godly father looks like.
q257: God made the brain with an alarm and a pilot. When we pause, breathe and step away, the alarm settles and the pilot, the prefrontal cortex, can take control again. Research suggests that naming an emotion can reduce activity in the brain's alarm centre. God also designed children's brains to calm down through a calm adult, which is called co-regulation. When a father repairs after a rupture, studies suggest the child learns that relationships can survive conflict. Because the brain can change, the anger patterns passed down from Sunil's father do not have to be passed on to his children.
q258: James 1:19|Wherefore, my beloved brethren, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath.
q262: Within two months the shouting dropped from almost every night to once or twice a month. Sunil still feels the heat rise, especially at the end of the month, and he still sometimes raises his voice. But now he steps away and comes back to repair. His daughter has stopped flinching. Recently his son said, Papa, you say sorry now.
q263: Anger is a signal pointing to what lies underneath, and repair can break patterns passed down for generations.
q264: When you feel angry, it is okay to stop and breathe. If you shout, you can say sorry, and that helps everyone feel safe again.
q265: Ananya and the drawing that was never finished
q266: Ananya, 31, architect at a design firm in Chennai, single, lives with her parents
q267: Ananya was known as the most talented architect in her firm, and also the slowest. She would redraw a floor plan twelve times, staying at the office till midnight, because the lines did not feel right. When a senior colleague pointed out a small error in her presentation, she could not sleep for three nights. She missed two deadlines, and her team lead asked if something was wrong. Ananya felt crushed. She told herself that if she could not be excellent, she should not do it at all. She stopped volunteering for new projects. Her mother kept saying God wants us to do our best, but to Ananya best always meant flawless. She was exhausted, and the joy she once had in design was gone.
q268: Perfectionism is not the same as high standards. Healthy striving says I want to do well. Perfectionism says I must not fail, or I am not acceptable. Ananya grew up as the topper in her family, praised for marks rather than for who she was. Her brain linked mistakes with danger to her belonging. When a mistake happened, her stress system fired as though she had been rejected. Research suggests perfectionism is linked with anxiety, burnout and procrastination, because the fear of imperfection makes starting and finishing feel unsafe. Her inner critic sounded like a strict teacher, and she believed it was keeping her sharp.
q269: At a retreat, a speaker asked everyone to write what they believed God thought of them when they failed. Ananya wrote, Disappointed. Then she read Psalm 103:14, He knoweth our frame, he remembereth that we are dust. She cried, realising she had expected herself to be more than human.
